Underwater Trash Rack Cleaning: Robotic Options, Risks and Acceptance Tests

How robotic trash-rack cleaning works, when it suits a hydropower intake, what to survey first and how to agree acceptance tests, with a crawler cleaning robot example.

By PanPan Marine · Published 30 October 2026 · 9 min read

The short answer

Robotic trash-rack cleaning uses a remotely operated vehicle that holds onto the rack and removes attached deposits — typically biological growth, shells or hardened sediment — with a water jet or brush. It suits deposits that fixed rakes cannot remove and situations where draining the intake or sending divers is costly or risky. It does not replace debris raking for large floating material. Survey the rack and deposit first, then agree a trial and acceptance test on a representative area.

1. Why trash racks foul

Trash racks protect turbines and pumps from debris, but the bars themselves collect material. Floating debris is usually handled by rake machines at the surface. Attached deposits — mussels and other biological growth, algae, calcified material or hardened sediment — build up on the bars below the waterline and increase head loss across the rack. Over time that costs generation and can load the rack structurally.

Traditional responses are lowering the water level, lifting racks out, or sending divers with hand tools. Each has cost, outage or safety implications, which is why owners look at robotic cleaning.

Head loss is the clearest signal. Many plants measure the water level difference across the rack; a rising difference at similar flow indicates growing blockage. Recording this before and after cleaning is also the simplest way to show the value of the work.

2. How robotic cleaning works

A cleaning robot is lowered to the rack, swims to the work area and holds onto the bars using thrust and tracks. It then moves systematically across the rack while a cleaning tool removes deposits. The A-80, for example, is a 100 kg crawler rated to 300 m that switches between swimming and crawling and cleans with a cavitation water jet or an interchangeable brush. The manufacturer lists teleoperated and supervised semi-autonomous control modes.

Cavitation water jets create collapsing vapour bubbles at the surface that break up deposits without the nozzle touching the bars. Brushes remove softer growth mechanically. The right tool depends on the deposit and on how much the bar coating can tolerate.

Holding onto a rack is different from holding onto a flat wall. The robot’s tracks or contact points must suit the bar spacing and profile, and the robot must be able to cross horizontal support members. Ask the supplier which rack geometries the robot has worked on and whether a trial on a sample rack section is possible before purchase.

3. When robotic cleaning fits — and when it does not

Good fitPoor fit
Attached biological growth or hard deposits below the waterlineLarge floating debris (logs, vegetation mats) — use raking
Racks that are hard to remove or drain behindBar spacing or geometry the robot cannot hold onto
Repeat cleaning on a scheduleOne-off cleaning where draining is already planned
Diver work that is costly or restrictedFlow that cannot be reduced during cleaning

A short review of these points with the plant’s mechanical and operations staff usually shows quickly whether a trial is worthwhile. If several items fall in the right-hand column, consider other methods first.

4. Survey the rack before you buy

Collect: rack drawings, bar spacing and profile, bar material and coating, rack angle and dimensions, water depth, typical and minimum flow, access for launching, and photographs or video of the deposits. A short inspection with a compact ROV such as the R-30 can document the deposit type and coverage before the cleaning system is specified.

The deposit is the single most important input. Soft growth, hard shells and calcified sediment respond very differently to water jets and brushes.

Record also the rack’s history: when it was last cleaned or replaced, how head loss has developed, and any damage found in previous inspections. Damaged or corroded bars change how cleaning should be approached and may need repair before cleaning is worthwhile.

5. Water jet, brush or both?

Cavitation water jets suit hard, firmly attached deposits and work without contact, which reduces the risk of the tool catching on bars. They need a high-pressure pump at the surface and a hose alongside the tether, and their effectiveness depends on standoff distance and nozzle design.

Brushes are simpler and suit softer growth such as algae and young biofouling. They apply mechanical force, which means reaction forces on the robot and a greater risk of wearing coatings if used aggressively. Some robots carry interchangeable tools so the method can be matched to each rack. Agree with the supplier which tool will be used for your deposit and why, and test both if the deposit is mixed.

Whichever tool is chosen, ask for its operating parameters to be recorded during the trial — pressure, standoff, travel speed — so that a successful setting can be repeated on later campaigns.

6. Flow and unit operation

Cleaning a rack while the unit runs at full flow is rarely practical: the robot must hold position against the flow and dislodged material is carried into the water passage. Most methods assume reduced flow or a unit shutdown for the cleaning period, without draining. Agree the flow limit, the isolation procedure and how dislodged material will be handled.

The manufacturer reports that, at the Baihetan hydropower station, the A-80 project cleaned intake racks without draining the water, stopping the facility or sending personnel underwater. Read our trash-rack case study for what that statement does and does not establish.

7. Support equipment

Cleaning robots need more surface equipment than inspection ROVs: a high-pressure pump for water-jet cleaning, hoses alongside the tether, a power supply, lifting equipment and a control station. Check the space at the intake deck, the power available and the route for hoses and tether to the rack.

For racks deep below the deck, check the lifting arrangement for the robot and the hose weight hanging below the deck. A long, water-filled high-pressure hose is heavy and needs proper support and strain relief. Plan how hoses and tether will be kept apart to prevent tangling.

8. Planning cleaning campaigns

Biological growth follows seasons. In many waters, growth is fastest in warmer months, so a cleaning campaign timed just after the peak growth season can hold head loss down for longer. Plants with several units can rotate cleaning through units during planned low-demand periods to avoid losing generation.

Record the area cleaned, the time taken and the head loss before and after on each campaign. Over two or three cycles the records show how quickly deposits return and whether the cleaning interval should be adjusted.

9. Agreeing acceptance tests

Agree, before the trial, how success will be measured:

  • Before-and-after video of marked areas at the same standoff and lighting.
  • Area cleaned per hour under the agreed flow conditions.
  • Residual deposit level that counts as “clean”.
  • Condition of bars and coatings after cleaning, checked on a representative area.
  • Head-loss readings before and after, where instrumentation allows.

Run the trial on a representative section, not the easiest one.

Write the agreed acceptance criteria into the purchase or service contract. If the trial fails to meet them, the contract should state what happens next: adjustment and a second trial, a change of tool, or withdrawal without further cost.

10. Risks to manage

  • Coating damage. Aggressive cleaning can remove protective coatings. Test first and agree limits.
  • Snagging. Tethers and hoses can catch on rack edges or debris. Plan routing and recovery.
  • Dislodged material. Decide whether it can pass downstream or must be collected.
  • Changing flow. Agree communication with the control room and stop criteria.

Write these risks into the method statement with a named response for each, and review the statement with the plant operator before mobilisation.

11. Team and training

A cleaning crew typically includes a pilot, a tether and hose tender, a pump operator and the plant’s representative. Operators need training on the robot, the cleaning tool and the plant’s safety procedures. Plan a familiarisation session on an accessible rack before working on a critical intake, and agree who maintains the pump and robot between campaigns.

12. See the concept

The manufacturer’s animation on the A-80 page shows wall-crawling motion and other intended uses such as gate leak detection and sealing and gate-slot obstacle clearing. It illustrates the concept; it is not project footage, and each additional use needs its own tools, procedure and site review.

13. Cleaning or dredging?

If the problem is loose sediment in front of the intake or in a sump rather than deposits on the bars, the task is dredging, not cleaning. Our guide to underwater cleaning versus dredging explains the difference, and the trash-rack cleaning guide covers the application in more depth.

14. Next step

Send rack drawings, deposit photographs and flow conditions with your project brief. A review of those inputs is the fastest way to know whether robotic cleaning fits your intake.

If the review suggests robotic cleaning fits, the next step is usually a site trial on one rack section with agreed measurements, followed by a decision on purchase or a campaign service. That sequence keeps the investment proportional to the evidence.

Frequently asked questions

Can a robot clean trash racks without draining the intake?

Often yes, with reduced flow or the unit shut down. The robot holds onto the rack underwater. Agree flow limits and procedures with the plant operator.

Does robotic cleaning replace rake machines?

No. Rake machines handle floating debris at the surface. Robots target attached deposits on the bars below the waterline.

Will a water jet damage the rack coating?

It can if settings are too aggressive. Test on a representative area and agree acceptable limits before full cleaning.

How fast can a robot clean a rack?

It depends on the deposit, bar geometry, flow and tool. Agree a measured trial rather than relying on a nominal figure.

What information is needed to assess a rack?

Drawings, bar spacing and profile, material and coating, dimensions and angle, depth, flow, access and images of the deposits.

Can the same robot inspect and clean?

A cleaning robot carries cameras and can record the rack before and after cleaning. For detailed inspection of large areas, a separate inspection ROV may still be quicker.
